turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: Good afternoon. I have a lot to catch you up on today. The biggest news is the private room project — Sala Modena construction underway, on schedule, which is a genuine relief. I was worried about timeline slippage after the permit delays we had back in April. The contractor confirmed this morning that we are still on track for an early September completion, which gives us just enough lead time to do a proper soft launch before we push into full marketing mode. I have been losing sleep over this project for the better part of three months, so being able to say the words 'on schedule' out loud feels significant. The original budget is also holding. We built in a twelve-percent contingency and at this point we have drawn less than half of it. I was mentally prepared for a worse number.

turns.speaker: Assistant
turns.text: That is genuinely good news on both the schedule and the budget, Kenta, and I understand why it is a relief. When you are running a capital project inside an operating restaurant, schedule risk always carries a multiplier effect on stress. A permit delay that pushes a September completion into October does not just cost you the room revenue for those weeks — it destabilizes every piece of downstream planning you have built around that date: marketing timelines, pre-booking commitments, staffing arrangements, the whole stack. So staying on schedule matters more than just the timeline itself. A contingency running under six percent at this stage of the build is also a good sign — it tells you the contractor is executing cleanly and that your cost estimates at the outset were well-grounded rather than optimistic. Let me ask: where are you physically in the build-out right now, and what are the remaining milestones between here and the contractor's handover date? Are there any items you are watching closely, or does everything feel clean at this stage?

turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: Physically, they have finished the structural work and the acoustic paneling is mostly in. The lighting rig is being installed this week — we went with the indirect warm system we discussed a few months ago, the one that gives you that almost candlelit quality without actually using candles, which matters for the insurance side of things. The biggest outstanding items are the custom millwork for the wine display cabinet and the upholstered wall sections in the far corners, which are being fabricated off-site and scheduled to arrive in the first week of August. If those come in on time, the contractor thinks we can have a walk-through punch list done by mid-August and hand the room over to us by August 28th at the latest. That gives us roughly a week for our own finishing and staging before we would be ready to host the first event. I have been thinking about doing a friends-and-family soft launch in the very first week of September, just to stress-test the room before we open it to paying guests. I want to discover whatever goes wrong when it does not cost me anything to fix it.

turns.speaker: Assistant
turns.text: The August 28th handover with a first-week-of-September soft launch is a tight but workable sequence, assuming the millwork arrives on schedule. The off-site fabrication items are your single biggest scheduling risk right now — custom millwork and upholstered pieces from fabricators are exactly the kind of items that slip by a week without much warning, and you are operating without a lot of buffer. I would want to know what the fabricator's confirmed delivery date is in writing, not just a verbal estimate relayed through the contractor, and whether there is a contingency plan if those pieces arrive in the second week of August rather than the first. Even a five-day slip compresses the punch list window and puts pressure on everything downstream. On the soft launch concept: a friends-and-family event in early September is the right instinct, and I would say it is almost essential given that you are commissioning a new room that has never been run under service conditions. You cannot fully anticipate from blueprints how the service route between the kitchen and the private space will feel under time pressure, whether the acoustics at a full seated table of twelve or fourteen produce any unexpected reflections, whether the lighting is actually doing what you want it to do when there are bodies and warm food in the room versus what it looked like in the empty mock-up, or whether the temperature settles correctly once you have a dozen guests and multiple courses running. None of that can be predicted in advance, and discovering it during a paid event is a much more expensive lesson. Who are you thinking you would invite, and how are you planning to structure the evening?

turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: I would probably do two seatings over two consecutive nights — one for industry people and a few journalist contacts I have built relationships with over the years, and one for close personal relationships and long-standing regulars who have been asking about the room since before construction even started. The industry night is partly operational testing and partly a soft signal to the market that Sala Modena exists and is worth knowing about. The regulars night is more personal — there are guests who have been eating at Osteria Morishita since we opened, people who watched the restaurant find its footing, and I want them to experience the room before it goes public. But here is where the conversation gets more complicated, because the pre-booking situation has moved faster than I anticipated. We started very quietly putting the word out about three weeks ago — not a formal launch, not any public communication, just a few direct conversations and some targeted outreach to a short list of contacts — and we already have 6 private events booked for September. Two of those are corporate, four are private celebrations. One is a fiftieth birthday dinner for twenty people that the guest's daughter organized and which I think will be a genuinely beautiful evening when it comes together. The September calendar is filling up faster than I expected, and I am a little nervous that the soft launch window is getting squeezed entirely.

turns.speaker: Assistant
turns.text: Six private events booked for September before you have even done a formal launch is a strong early signal — it tells you that the concept is landing with the people you reached out to, and that there is genuine pent-up demand for a dedicated private dining option in Higashi-Azabu at this positioning. The fiftieth birthday dinner for twenty is particularly valuable as an early booking because large celebration events tend to be high-spend, high-engagement evenings that generate word-of-mouth in exactly the social circles you want Sala Modena to become associated with. The daughter who organized it will almost certainly tell people who planned it when the evening goes well, and that kind of organic referral from a personal network is worth more than most marketing spend. The squeeze on the soft launch window is real, though. If you have 6 private events for September and the handover is August 28th, you have at most a few days of internal use before you are running live events. That changes the risk calculus significantly. The soft launch was supposed to be your error-absorbing buffer — the place where you discover that the service route between the kitchen and the private room adds four minutes to each course, or that the wine refrigeration unit is louder than expected when the room is quiet. Now that buffer is essentially gone. How are you thinking about handling that operationally?

turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: My current thinking is that we do one very tight internal dinner — just me, Petrelli, and the full front-of-house team — as a complete service rehearsal in the last few days of August. We run it exactly like a real event: full menu, full wine service, timed sequences, the whole thing. Petrelli can be a demanding critic when the shoe is on the other foot, which is actually useful in this context. I will ask him to behave like a difficult guest and find every friction point he can. But I want to tell you about the most significant booking we have, because it is the one that is shaping how I am thinking about everything else. Marubeni booked Sala Modena for October 14 for a 14-person dinner. Former employer. The person who made the booking is a senior director in the corporate strategy division — not someone I worked directly with, but someone who knows my background well enough to have formed a view on my decision to open the restaurant. This is not a booking I can have any hiccups on. The September events matter, but this is the one I will measure myself against.

turns.speaker: Assistant
turns.text: The Marubeni booking on October 14 for a 14-person dinner is significant on multiple levels and I want to make sure we are thinking about it carefully rather than just treating it as another entry on the calendar. First, the business dimension: Marubeni is a major general trading company, and a 14-person dinner from the corporate strategy division is almost certainly an entertainment booking — external clients, internal leadership, or a combination — which means every person in that room is simultaneously a guest and an implicit evaluator. They are forming a view on whether Sala Modena is a venue they would recommend to a peer at another company, use again for a different group, or simply remember as an exceptional experience. One flawless dinner on October 14 could plant a reference that generates corporate bookings for years at no additional marketing cost. Second, and I think this matters more than the direct business case: the fact that they know your background and chose to book with you is a statement of a particular kind. People who watched you leave a trading company career to open a restaurant in Higashi-Azabu had a range of reactions at the time, and the ones who now book Sala Modena for a corporate strategy dinner are making a visible choice about how they see what you have built. That is not pressure in the negative sense — it is confirmation. But it does mean the evening deserves a level of preparation that goes beyond your standard operating excellence. How did the booking actually come through — did they reach out to you, or did you make the first approach?

turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: They reached out to me, which was the part that genuinely surprised me. I had put Osteria Morishita on their preferred vendor list for corporate dining about a year ago through an administrative contact, and it had been completely quiet on that front ever since. Then about ten days ago I got a message from an assistant to the director saying they were interested in the private room for a fall dinner. I had not specifically promoted Sala Modena to Marubeni directly — it was more a case of the word having traveled through some connection I am not fully aware of, possibly through one of the corporate bookings we hosted in the main dining room last spring. But I was very direct in the response about pricing and the scope of what we offer, because I do not want any ambiguity going into a booking like this. I quoted our terms plainly: 18,000 yen per person minimum, venue fee 50,000 yen, in exactly that language, so there is no room for a misunderstanding when the invoice arrives. They confirmed without pushback. At 14 people, that is already a substantial evening at minimum spend, and my expectation is that the actual spend will run considerably above the minimum once you factor in the full dinner format and wine. I also told them we would prepare a custom welcome letter with the director's name and a brief note about the menu concept, which I think signals the level of personal attention they can expect.

turns.speaker: Assistant
turns.text: The fact that they confirmed the pricing without pushback is itself informative — it tells you that a senior director in corporate strategy at Marubeni is calibrated to fine dining entertainment at that level of expenditure, and that your pricing structure is not a friction point for corporate clients in that tier. Being explicit about the terms in the way you were is exactly right for a booking of this nature. Any ambiguity about pricing with a former employer would be a particularly uncomfortable conversation to have after the fact, so the fact that it is settled and documented before we are even into August is clean. Let us look at the arithmetic plainly. At 14 people with 18,000 yen per person minimum, venue fee 50,000 yen, the guaranteed floor for the evening is 302,000 yen before a single supplemental course or bottle of wine is ordered. In practice, a corporate strategy group entertaining in a private room at a restaurant of this positioning will almost always take a wine pairing — it is part of what they are paying for, and it is the kind of choice that signals to the guests that the evening was properly resourced. Wine pairings start at 6,500 yen per person, so if every guest takes only the entry-level pairing and nothing more, that adds 91,000 yen on top of the minimum. Realistically, a group at that seniority level will run higher than the entry pairing, and there will likely be supplemental courses as well, so the actual total will probably land well above 400,000 yen. That is a meaningful evening on its own terms, and it also sets a benchmark for what you can credibly propose to other corporate accounts when you begin outreach later in the fall. What are you thinking about for the menu itself on October 14?

turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: I have already started thinking about the menu in some detail. For a group like this I want to do something that is classic in its overall structure but where every individual element is clearly a deliberate choice — not a cautious menu that hedges toward the inoffensive, but a confident menu that shows exactly what we do and why. Petrelli and I have been discussing a twelve-course progression where the first half leans into the autumn vegetables and game birds that are genuinely at peak in mid-October in Japan — matsutake, sudachi, roasted squash preparations, quail — and the second half builds toward a dry-aged beef course that we are hoping to source from a small family producer in Tochigi that we have been in conversation with for about six weeks. If that sourcing comes together, and I think it will by the time we need to commit, that course alone will be something that most people in the room will not have encountered prepared in quite that way. The aging profile the Tochigi producer uses is different from anything we have served before. The wine question is the one I am spending the most time on, because a Marubeni corporate strategy group at that seniority level will almost certainly have people in the room who know wine seriously — I would assume at least two or three people who have spent extended time in Europe for work and have strong opinions. I do not want to run a pairing that feels like the standard house progression. I am seriously considering bringing in an external sommelier consultant for that specific event — someone who has direct corporate entertainment experience and who can handle a more bespoke and genuinely conversational interaction with guests if the evening goes in that direction. On my own personal presence in the room: I will greet them when they arrive, introduce the concept of the evening briefly, then leave them to it. I will come back at the midpoint to check in without making it feel like an inspection, and again near the end to close the evening personally. That is a dinner where my visibility needs to feel completely natural and unforced — the moment it feels managed, it becomes something else.

turns.speaker: Kenta
turns.text: But I want to step back from the Marubeni event specifically and think about the broader marketing picture, because that is one booking and what I really need is an approach for Sala Modena that builds a consistent pipeline of corporate and private bookings on a repeatable basis going into 2027. Right now the 6 private events for September happened through word of mouth and my direct personal network, and I am genuinely grateful for that early traction, but it is not a scalable or predictable source of business. There is a version of this where I do well in September and October because of relationships I built over fifteen years at Marubeni and in Tokyo's food community, but then struggle in February when those networks have been tapped and there is no structured pipeline behind them. That is the scenario I want to avoid. I have three ideas I have been turning over, and I want your honest reaction to all three before I commit to a direction. The first is a targeted direct outreach program specifically aimed at HR directors and the networks of executive assistants at large Tokyo corporations — because those are the actual decision-makers on private dining reservations. It is almost never the executive whose name appears on the booking who chose the venue. It is the EA, or the HR event manager, or the department coordinator who maintains the shortlist. The second is building a Sala Modena-dedicated page on the Osteria Morishita website with comprehensive information about the room — photographs, capacity range, the full pricing structure laid out plainly, the format options we support, and a clear way to make an inquiry. Right now the main site has barely more than a sentence acknowledging that a private room exists. And the third is exploring whether to pursue press coverage, specifically targeting the corporate entertaining angle through publications and writers that reach the senior businesspeople in Tokyo who actually control entertainment budgets. What is your read on priority order for all three, and is there anything I am missing?

turns.speaker: Assistant
turns.text: All three are legitimate channels, and I would eventually want you executing all of them — but the sequencing matters a great deal, and the right order is probably not the one that feels most immediately satisfying to work on. Let me give you my honest read on each. The Sala Modena website page is first. Not first among equals, not running in parallel with something else — genuinely first, and completed before you accelerate any of the other channels. Here is the logic: every other marketing action you take will eventually send someone to the internet to verify what they heard or to share a link with the person who controls the decision. The corporate EA who got your name from a colleague at another company, the journalist researching a piece on private dining in Tokyo, the Marubeni director sharing the October 14 booking details with his team — all of them will at some point go to the Osteria Morishita website to look up Sala Modena. Right now that search produces a brief mention and essentially nothing else. When a venue page does not give an evaluator what they need, the friction almost always resolves in favor of looking at a competitor who did make the information available. The page needs to convey the room clearly enough that someone can make a meaningful judgment without a site visit: capacity range for both seated dinners and standing receptions, physical dimensions in a way that lets a person visualize how their group will fit, the complete pricing structure — and I would state the 18,000 yen per person minimum and the venue fee 50,000 yen in exactly that language, the way you quoted it to Marubeni, because transparency at this stage of the consideration process builds trust rather than reducing it — and the wine options, including that wine pairings start at 6,500 yen so a client can estimate the total before picking up the phone. Photographs are essential and they need to be excellent: not phone photos of an empty room, but properly lit professional images that show the space as it looks during service. This page is probably four to six weeks of focused work if you do it properly, and it is the foundation that every other channel depends on. The direct outreach to HR directors and EA networks is your second move and it is the activity with the highest return per unit of effort once the website page is live. Executive assistants who manage entertainment budgets at large companies are systematically undervalued as a channel in fine dining because the industry instinct is to reach the principal — the executive, the director, the partner — when in practice the EA is the one maintaining the shortlist, handling the logistics, making the initial inquiry, and often having the decisive influence on which venues make it into rotation. If you can get into the working memory of five or six EAs at firms with active corporate entertainment programs, and if those EAs have one excellent experience with Sala Modena to anchor their recommendation, the referral behavior compounds over time at essentially no ongoing marketing cost. I would time the start of this outreach to October, after you have a handful of the September events behind you and genuine operational confidence in the room. The Marubeni dinner on October 14 is particularly useful in that context — after that evening, you have a named reference that any EA in the corporate world will recognize, and that changes the credibility of the outreach conversation meaningfully. Press is third, and I would be deliberate rather than urgent about it. The path from a reader encountering a piece about private dining in Tokyo to making a Sala Modena reservation is long and indirect — you are investing in brand awareness that may pay off months later and in ways that are difficult to attribute. Press is worth doing, but publication selection matters enormously. You want writers and editors covering corporate entertaining, premium event spaces, or expense-account dining in Tokyo, not the general restaurant review circuit, which reaches a food-curious audience that is a different type of buyer entirely. Late November or December is the natural timing for press outreach — you will have a full first quarter of Sala Modena operations behind you, real events you can reference by type and scale, and a story that is about established momentum rather than an opening announcement. On whether there is anything missing from your list: one additional channel worth considering is a lightweight referral acknowledgment for existing guests who bring corporate groups to the room. Not a formal commission arrangement — something simpler, like a reserved priority booking window for guests who have referred a private event to Sala Modena within the past year. It is a small operational addition that gives your most engaged existing clients a tangible reason to mention the room to their networks, which is exactly the word-of-mouth behavior that filled your September calendar before you even had a formal marketing program in place.
